text:
Recent work separates explanation fluency, factual support, and preference alignment. [Shimizu et al. (WWW 2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.13248) show that strong text-similarity metrics do not ensure alignment with user likes/dislikes; their method requires reviews unavailable here. [Wardatzky et al. (RecSys 2026)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01627) find moderate human–LLM ranking correlation but low absolute agreement; neither reliably detects unsupported explanations. Implication: audit claims against permitted evidence rather than treating persuasive explanations as preference evidence.

Proposed diagnostic taxonomy: ambiguous item identity; unsupported descriptive claim; broad topical match without specific history support; textual redundancy within recommendations; support concentrated in one isolated interaction versus repeated/recent interactions. Measure normalized title/description overlap, pairwise list similarity, supporting-history counts, and timestamp gaps; retain supporting item IDs and text spans. These are observable proxies, not proof of dislike, ownership, compatibility, or useful complementarity. Require explicit user feedback for those judgments; otherwise label unknown. Distinguish textual repetition from user-confirmed unwanted redundancy.

For twenty users, use a short codebook, pilot examples, two independent annotators, evidence spans, and an insufficient-evidence option. Report pre-adjudication raw agreement and Krippendorff’s alpha per label, preserving disagreements; [Klie et al. (2024)](https://aclanthology.org/2024.cl-3.1/) document common agreement-measurement errors. Evaluate abstention through coverage and error among retained judgments, consistent with [2026 abstention-aware evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.14189). Treat confidence calibration as exploratory: show counts and user-level uncertainty intervals rather than fine confidence bins. Keep these qualitative diagnostics separate from the pinned macro validation HR@10 used for selection.
